definition: The legal authority of the ICC to investigate and prosecute crimes. The ICC has jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.
context: The ICC can only exercise jurisdiction if the crime was committed on the territory of a State Party, or by a national of a State Party, or if the UN Security Council refers the situation.

definition: The principle that the ICC complements, rather than replaces, national criminal justice systems. The ICC can only intervene when national courts are unwilling or unable to genuinely investigate or prosecute.
context: This means the ICC does not replace national jurisdiction but acts when national systems fail to do so.

definition: The process of gathering and examining information and evidence by the ICC Prosecutor. An investigation is distinct from charges or a judicial finding of guilt.
context: Authorization to investigate does not mean that charges will be filed, or that any individual has been found guilty of any crime.

definition: The criteria the ICC uses to determine whether a case can be heard. A case must be of sufficient gravity and the State must be unwilling or unable to genuinely investigate or prosecute.
A fundamental principle that anyone accused of a crime is presumed innocent until proven guilty in a fair trial. This applies to all ICC proceedings.
context: Investigation, or even charges, do not constitute a finding of guilt.

definition: A judicial order issued by the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber authorizing the arrest of an individual. It requires reasonable grounds to believe the person committed crimes within ICC jurisdiction.
context: A warrant is not a conviction. It is issued to secure the appearance of an accused person before the Court.

definition: Formal accusations of criminal conduct brought by the Prosecutor and confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber. Charges must be proven beyond reasonable doubt at trial.
The judicial process where evidence is presented, examined, and tested before a panel of judges. The accused has the right to a fair and public hearing.
A judicial finding of guilt by the Trial Chamber, made only after the Prosecutor proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
A judicial finding that the accused is not guilty. The accused must be released immediately.
